entries.example: Velocity is speed with a direction: the athlete covers 100 metres in 20 seconds for a speed of 5 metres per second, and running right makes it a velocity of 5 metres per second rightwards.
entries.meaning: Distance travelled per unit time, calculated as distance divided by time, measured in metres per second.

entries.example: Check the thinking: the runner covers 800 metres in 100 seconds for a speed of 8 metres per second, but ends at the start, so displacement and velocity are both zero.
entries.meaning: Speed with a direction: displacement divided by time, so a round trip back to the start has zero average velocity.

entries.example: Check the thinking: the runner covers 800 metres in 100 seconds for a speed of 8 metres per second, but ends at the start, so displacement and velocity are both zero.
entries.meaning: The straight-line change in position from start to finish, with a direction - not the total path length.

entries.example: Velocity-time graphs: the line rises from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, so the slope is an acceleration of 2 metres per second squared, while the shaded area growing under the line is the 100 metres travelled.
entries.meaning: The rate of change of velocity, read off a velocity-time graph as its gradient.

entries.example: A distance-time graph climbs in a straight line: 120 metres in 60 seconds. Speed = gradient = 120 / 60 = 2 m/s. Check the units: metres divided by seconds gives metres per second, and the straight line means that speed never changes.
entries.meaning: Rise over run on a graph: on a distance-time graph it is the speed, and on a velocity-time graph it is the acceleration.

entries.example: Velocity-time graphs: the line rises from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, so the slope is an acceleration of 2 metres per second squared, while the shaded area growing under the line is the 100 metres travelled.
entries.meaning: The product of velocity and time accumulated under the line, which equals the distance travelled.
